newsitem.title: Angola: Diana, "princess of peace", sees Angolan war victims.
newsitem.headline: Diana, "princess of peace", sees Angolan war victims.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana earned herself the name "princess of peace" on Tuesday when she met war victims in the poorest quarters of Angola's capital Luanda and promised to send toys to comfort the children.

On day two of a four-day tour of the southern African country, to help a Red Cross campaign to outlaw landmines worldwide, she came face to face for the first time with the casualties of a bitter 20-year war that ended in 1994.
At a pioneering orthopaedic centre at Neves Bendinha on the city outskirts, she chatted with ex-combatants and children waiting to be fitted with artificial limbs.

Diana, in workaday short khaki trousers, a sleeveless blue shirt and moccasins, watched as the youngest patient Sandra Tigica, 11, was fitted with an artificial leg. She lost her leg in an air raid in the closing days of the war.
"The princess asked what she can give me for support, and I told her a toy. I have no toys," Tigica told Reuters. She said Diana had promised to send her one.

Outside, former soldiers who lost limbs in landmine explosions waited to see the princess whose importance, though she is little known here, was obvious to all who saw the hordes of journalists following her.
"We would like to get to know her because she is the princess of peace," said 22-year-old Bernado Cupemula.
There are still nine million mines -- one for each Angolan. Angola has three amputees per 1,000 people, the world's highest rate, and some 24 new victims are admitted to hospital each day.
Outside the grounds of the centre, members of Angola's "ban landmines campaign" waved a banner calling for a total ban.

"We are not protesting, but we want to make clear that it is not enough to send money to help victims of mines," one said. "That is addressing the symptoms, not the problem. What is needed is a total ban on landmines."

Earlier Diana, 35, visited a medical post for pregnant women run by the International Federation of the Red Cross in dirt-poor Kikolo suburb, where most of Luanda's two million war displaced people live in squalid conditions.

She sat down to talk to Dominga Manuel, 58, who lost her leg in a mine accident in 1974 as the civil war between U.S.- and Cuban-backed parties simmered. Portugal gave its colony an unplanned independence the next year and the fighting raged.
"I told her the situation of our lives, I have children but I have nothing to give them," Manuel told Reuters later.
In the afternoon the Princess met the United Nations special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, for hour-long talks on the landmine situation.

The United Nations, overseeing the implementation of the 1994 peace pact between the government and former rebel UNITA, has helped to demine 5,000 km (3,125 miles) of roads to help people to move freely between provinces.
During the talks Diana was given a detonated anti-personnel mine by the U.N. landmine programme coordinator Peter Isaacs, also a victim of a mine blast.
"The princess said she would visit other countries with landmine problems. I gave her an anti-personnel mine I hope she will keep on her desk," Isaacs told Reuters.
On Wednesday Diana will wear body armour to visit a minefield in a remote part of the country.

Her Angola visit could help revive a public image that was sullied by last year's bitter divorce from heir to the throne Prince Charles. Royal watchers predict more high-profile charity work could follow.
